Good morning, everyone. Pencils down and eyes on me, please. Let's warm up our brains. If I cut a sandwich into two equal pieces and eat one piece, what fraction did I eat? One half! One half, well done. And if I cut it into four equal pieces and eat one? One quarter. Yes. Sam, which is bigger, one half or one quarter? One half, because when you cut it into two, the pieces are bigger than when you cut it into four. Exactly. Fewer equal parts means bigger parts. Now look at the board. Our objective today is: we will add fractions with the same denominator. Let's read it together. We will add fractions with the same denominator. Lovely. Everyone take one paper strip from the tray. It is marked into five equal parts, so fold along each line. Each part is one fifth. Now shade one part. Then shade two more parts. How many fifths are shaded? Three fifths. Three fifths. So one fifth plus two fifths makes three fifths. The parts stay the same size, they are still fifths, we just have more of them. Now, someone once told me one fifth plus two fifths is three tenths. Hands up if you agree. Hmm, a few hands. Ayo, look at your strip. Did it get cut into ten parts? No, it's still five parts. They are the same size as before. Right. The denominator tells us the size of the parts, and the size does not change, so we never add the denominators. Watch me on the board. One fifth plus two fifths. Step one, check the denominators match: five and five. Step two, add the numerators: one plus two is three. Step three, keep the denominator. Three fifths. Now let's do some together. Two eighths plus three eighths. Are the denominators the same? Yes! Two plus three is five. Five eighths. Good. Next: one sixth plus four sixths. Everyone? Five sixths. Sam, how did you know? One plus four is five, and it stays sixths. Perfect. Now work with your partner. Your card has three problems: two sevenths plus three sevenths, one quarter plus two quarters, and three tenths plus four tenths. Use your strips to show each one, then write the answer. Three minutes. Lina, please share your strips with Tomi. We got five sevenths for the first one, because two plus three is five. Teacher, is three quarters right for the second one? Show me on your strip. One quarter, two more quarters... yes, three quarters. Well done, both of you. Time's up. Swap your card with the pair behind you. Check their answers with your strips. Tick if you agree, and talk to them if you don't. They wrote seven twentieths for the last one. I think they added the bottom numbers. Ah, what did they do? They added the denominators. Help them fix it. Good. Now, mini whiteboards. Write three ninths plus four ninths. Show me in three, two, one, show! Seven ninths! I see lots of seven ninths. Thumbs up if you feel confident, sideways if you're nearly there. Mostly thumbs up, great. Who can tell me today's rule in one sentence? When the denominators are the same, add the numerators and keep the denominator. Brilliant. Everyone say it with them. Now your exit ticket: one question each. Two sixths plus three sixths.
